title: Grade 1 Addition Word Problems: Turn Any Story Into a Sum + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 1 Addition Word Problems (Easy Method) + Quiz
meta_desc: Turn Grade 1 addition word problems into number sentences with a simple 5-step method, four worked examples and a free 8-question quiz for your child.
excerpt: Most six-year-olds can add 7 and 5 on paper but freeze when the same sum is hidden inside a story about mangoes. Here is the read-find-spot-write-check method I use to turn any Grade 1 story into a number sentence, with four worked examples.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a scene every parent of a six-year-old will recognise. Your child races through a page of sums — 7 + 5, 8 + 6, 9 + 4 — getting nearly all of them right. Then you read out, ‘Aarav had 7 marbles and his sister gave him 5 more,’ and the same child stares at you as if the question were in another language. The arithmetic has not changed. The wrapping has. Grade 1 addition word problems are hard not because the numbers are big, but because the child has to find the sum before they can solve it.

The good news: turning a story into a number sentence is a teachable skill, not a talent. I use the same five-step routine with every child, and once it becomes a habit the panic disappears. You need no worksheets to start — just a story and a pencil.

The read-find-spot-write-check method

The whole method fits in five short steps. Say them out loud with your child until they can run through them without your help.

  • Read the story twice. The first read is for the picture; the second is for the numbers.
  • Find the numbers and underline them. In Grade 1 there are almost always exactly two.
  • Spot the action word — the clue that tells you what is happening.
  • Write the number sentence, then work out the answer.
  • Check that the answer makes sense and matches the question asked.

Why ‘spot the action word’ is the whole game

The single skill that decides whether a child gets word problems right is reading the action word. Certain words almost always signal addition: altogether, in all, total, both, more, and, joined, gave him. When a story says two groups come together or one group grows, you add. Teach your child to circle that word before doing anything else. It is the difference between a confident answer and a wild guess.

Four worked examples within 20

Watch the method run on real Grade 1 stories. Notice that the number sentence is written out fully before any counting happens — that order matters.

Example 1 — the mango basket

‘Meera picked 8 mangoes in the morning and 6 more in the evening. How many mangoes did she pick in all?’

Read it twice. Find the numbers: 8 and 6. Spot the action words: more and in all — both shout addition. Write the sentence: 8 + 6 = ? Now solve it by making ten — take 2 from the 6 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 4, so 10 + 4 = 14. Check: 14 mangoes is more than she started with, which fits a story about picking more. The answer is 14 mangoes.

Example 2 — marbles at the park

‘Rohan had 9 marbles. His friend gave him 5 more. How many marbles does Rohan have now?’

Numbers: 9 and 5. Action words: gave him and more — the group is growing, so we add. Sentence: 9 + 5 = ? Make ten: 1 from the 5 turns 9 into 10, leftover 4, so 10 + 4 = 14. Rohan has 14 marbles.

Example 3 — rupees in the piggy bank

‘Sara saved ₹7 last week and ₹8 this week. How much has she saved altogether?’

Numbers: 7 and 8. Action word: altogether — a clear addition signal. Sentence: 7 + 8 = ? This is a near-double: double 7 is 14, and one more makes 15. Sara has saved ₹15.

Example 4 — classmates on the bus

‘There were 6 girls and 7 boys on the school bus. How many children were on the bus?’

Numbers: 6 and 7. Action word: and, with the question asking for the total of two groups — addition. Sentence: 6 + 7 = ? Near-double again: double 6 is 12, plus 1 is 13. There were 13 children on the bus.

The trap that catches every child: the wrong operation

The most common mistake in Grade 1 is not a counting slip. It is choosing to subtract when the story wants addition, or the reverse. A child who has learned that ‘the word more always means add’ will trip on a story like ‘Priya has 5 sweets. She needs 3 more to have enough. How many will she have?’ — here more genuinely does mean add, so she is fine. But keyword-spotting is a helper, not a law. The real safeguard is the picture in the child’s head: are two groups coming together, or is one group being taken away? Always ask, ‘Is the answer going to be bigger or smaller than the numbers in the story?’ For addition it must be bigger. That one sanity check catches most wrong-operation errors before they land on the page.

Action words at a glance

Word in the storyWhat it usually meansExample phrase
altogether / in allAdd the groupsHow many in all?
more / and moreThe group grows — addgave him 5 more
both / totalCombine two amountsboth baskets together
and (two groups)Join and add6 girls and 7 boys
left / took awayUsually subtract — pause hereate 3, how many left

A ten-minute practice routine that works

In my experience teaching six-year-olds, the fastest progress comes from making your child the storyteller. After a week of solving stories, flip it: give them the sentence 7 + 6 = 13 and ask them to invent a story that fits — about their own cricket cards, their sister’s bangles, rupees for an ice cream. Children who can build a word problem can always solve one, because they finally see the machinery from the inside. Keep it to ten minutes, use their real world, and never rush the ‘read twice’ step. One honest caveat: resist the urge to read the whole problem for them once they can decode simple words. The reading is the maths here.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a short, free quiz built entirely from Grade 1 addition word problems — short stories with sums within 20, in the same everyday settings your child knows. Let them run the read-find-spot-write-check method on each one, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end of this page gives graded story sums with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Addition Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight short story sums, all within 20. Read each one twice, spot the action word, then pick your answer and press Check my score.

questions.q: Meera picked 8 mangoes in the morning and 6 more in the evening. How many did she pick in all?
questions.explanation: The words 'more' and 'in all' mean add. 8 + 6: make ten to get 10 + 4 = 14 mangoes.

questions.q: Rohan had 9 marbles. His friend gave him 5 more. How many does he have now?
questions.explanation: 'Gave him more' means the group grows, so add. 9 + 5 = 14 marbles.

questions.q: Sara saved ₹7 last week and ₹8 this week. How much altogether?
questions.explanation: 'Altogether' means add. 7 + 8 is a near-double: double 7 is 14, plus 1 is ₹15.

questions.q: There were 6 girls and 7 boys on the bus. How many children in total?
questions.explanation: Two groups joined by 'and', asking for the total, so add. 6 + 7 = 13 children.

questions.q: A shop had 10 red balloons and 4 blue balloons. How many balloons altogether?
questions.explanation: 'Altogether' means add the two groups. 10 + 4 = 14 balloons.

questions.q: Aarav read 5 pages before lunch and 5 pages after. How many pages in all?
questions.explanation: 'In all' means add. This is a double: 5 + 5 = 10 pages.

questions.q: Which word in a story usually tells you to add?
questions.explanation: 'Altogether' signals combining two groups, which means addition. 'Left' and 'took away' usually mean subtract.

questions.q: Priya had 8 stickers and her mother gave her 7 more. How many now?
questions.explanation: 'Gave her more' means add. 8 + 7: make ten to get 10 + 5 = 15 stickers.

faq.q: Why can my child do sums but not word problems?
faq.a: Because a word problem asks them to find the sum before solving it. The arithmetic is the easy part; reading the story, picking out the two numbers and choosing the right operation is the real work. Practise the finding, not just the adding.

faq.q: What words tell a Grade 1 child to add?
faq.a: The reliable signals are 'altogether', 'in all', 'total', 'both', 'more' and two groups joined by 'and'. Teach your child to circle that word first — but always check that the answer should be bigger than the numbers in the story.

faq.q: How do I stop my child choosing the wrong operation?
faq.a: Ask one question every time: will the answer be bigger or smaller than the numbers in the story? If two groups come together, it is bigger, so you add. That sanity check catches most wrong-operation mistakes before they reach the page.

faq.q: Should I read the word problem for my child?
faq.a: Read it with them at first, twice each time. Once they can decode simple words, let them read it themselves — the reading is part of the maths. Only step in for a word they genuinely cannot sound out.
